reason: A moss costa can differ in size, for example reduced or unequal. One example, 'dividing laminae unequally', is about the laminae, not the costa.
The alar region or group of alar cells can be triangular. The shape belongs to the group, not to a single cell, but it is meaningful.
A spathe can be narrow. Some examples, such as 'margin narrow', describe a sub-part, but the pair itself is sound.
A perianth can be small. The examples are annotated correctly.
Alar cells are described as well or poorly differentiated from the other cells. The examples match.
Anthers can be subcircular or subrotund in outline.
A leaf lobe can bear stiff bristle hairs (setose). 'Not setose' is a negation of the same quality.
A tree crown can be short, meaning low in height. The examples are correct.
The examples describe a sharp-pointed apex or teeth, not the sepal as a whole. A rule would need to map 'sharp-pointed apex' to an acute apex shape and leave the sepal itself out.
An involucre can be narrow. The examples about apices and lips are wrong-part cases, but the involucre ones are fine.
The abaxial epidermis or surface of a bract can be sericeous (silky hairs). The examples match.
A pedicel can be flexible or floppy.
Axils can be woolly (lanate), a common description.
Seed surfaces or seed coat cells can be domed. Some examples describe the cell walls or the domes, but the pair is meaningful.
Nodding (nutant) buds map to drooping.
A stigma lobe has a shape. 'Covered with mammillae' is a wrong reading, but the pair is valid.
A leaf blade can be subtriangular.
A leaf blade can be rectangular. Some examples are about cells, which is a wrong-part reading, but the pair is valid.
A spathe margin can be undulate (wavy). The pair is meaningful.

Occurrence in PATO means presence or absence. 'Interrupted or continuous' describes whether the arrangement of flowers along the axis is continuous, which is a wrong reading. It needs a separate continuity quality.
A sorus sits in a subterminal position on a vein. The examples match.
Bark can be deciduous, meaning it is shed.
Plant sap or latex can be watery.
The examples describe branching ('forked or pinnate') and relief ('flattened to raised'), not shape. A rule would need to send branching to a branching quality and relief to a surface-relief quality.

A strobilus can be asymmetric. The examples ('asymmetric at base', 'often asymmetric') look like leaf descriptions that were assigned to the strobilus, and only one flora supports the pair. A rule would need to check which part the text describes.
A tree crown can be irregularly shaped.

Position fits a pollinium only when it describes where the pollinium lies. 'Remaining enclosed in anther sacs' is a different reading, and 'horizontal to suberect' belongs to another part. A rule would need to separate enclosure and orientation from position.
A nectary can be conspicuous or inconspicuous.
Tepals can overlap (imbricate arrangement).
Sheath cells can be rectangular.
A peristome tooth can be acute or blunt, which is sharpness.
A leaf margin can be translucent.
A leaflet can be glaucous or pruinose (waxy bloom).
A labellum lobe can be lanceolate.
This quality covers shiny versus dull, which applies to leaf surfaces. Colour words in the examples belong to a colour quality, not this one.
Hairs or their septa can be colourless.
'Irregular' for a corolla means zygomorphic or not radially symmetric. PATO 'irregular spatial pattern' is a different meaning, so it is a wrong reading. It should map to a symmetry quality.
A spikelet can be fusiform.
A style can be woolly (lanate).
A leaf surface can be areolate. Some examples describe white areolae as separate structures, but the pair is valid.
Thorns, spines or prickles can be dense, which describes how closely they are spaced.
Suberect carpels map to semi erect.
A nectary scale has a 2-D shape, for example spatulate or quadrangular.
Roots can be twisted.
A mericarp can be grooved.
'Characteristic' is the root PATO quality, far too generic. The examples are really margin shape and size, so they belong to other qualities.
A style can be filamentous (thread-like).
Setae can be clustered or aggregated.
A prophyll can be obtuse at its apex.
Achenes can be reflexed. The examples include a negation, which is fine.
A stipule can be filamentous.
Pappus scales or elements can be toothed (dentate).
A labellum lobe can be quadrangular or subsquare.
An involucre can be sessile (without a stalk).
A reduced or abortive gynoecium or pistil can be small.
Branches of the inflorescence can be suberect.
A carpel can be covered with silky (sericeous) hairs.
A ray flower is not described as quadrangular. '4-angled' most likely refers to the achene or stem, so this is a wrong-part reading.
An indusium margin or the indusium itself can be flat. The examples match.
A corolla lip can be immobile or movable, for example in some orchids and Lamiaceae. The examples match.
